# Palindrome, Ignoring the Noise — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/two-pointers/valid-palindrome.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Two Pointers** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-palindrome/)

Given a string, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards once every non-alphanumeric character is ignored and case is disregarded.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= s.length <= 2 * 10^5
- s may contain letters, digits, spaces and punctuation
- a string with no alphanumeric characters at all is an empty palindrome — true, not false
- case is not part of the comparison, so 'A' and 'a' are the same character

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` | `true` | Strip the noise and it reads amanaplanacanalpanama. |
| `s = " "` | `true` | Nothing left to compare, so it is trivially a palindrome. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Two indices, one at each end, walking toward each other. What has to be true at every meeting?
2. Punctuation is not a mismatch — it is something to skip. Advance the pointer without comparing.
3. Skip first, compare second. If you compare before skipping, a comma will fail a perfectly good palindrome.

</details>

---

## 1. Clean, then reverse

Build a lowercase copy holding only the letters and digits, then check it against its own reverse.

```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    cleaned = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()]
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) b.append(Character.toLowerCase(c));
    }
    String cleaned = b.toString();
    return cleaned.equals(b.reverse().toString());
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool isPalindrome(const string& s) {
    string cleaned;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (isalnum((unsigned char)c)) cleaned += (char)tolower((unsigned char)c);
    }
    string flipped(cleaned.rbegin(), cleaned.rend());
    return cleaned == flipped;
}
```

</details>

---

## 2. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Building a cleaned copy spends O(n) memory to hold a string you read exactly once. Two indices read the original in place and stop the moment they disagree, so a mismatch in the first two characters costs two comparisons instead of a full rebuild.

Put i at the front and j at the back. Advance i past anything that is not alphanumeric, retreat j the same way, then compare the two characters case-insensitively. A disagreement ends it; a match moves both inward. When the pointers cross, every mirrored pair has agreed and the answer is true — including the case where they cross immediately because the string held no letters at all.

```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(i))) i++;
        while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(j))) j--;
        if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(i)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(j))) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool isPalindrome(const string& s) {
    int i = 0, j = (int)s.size() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        while (i < j && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[i])) i++;
        while (i < j && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[j])) j--;
        if (tolower((unsigned char)s[i]) != tolower((unsigned char)s[j])) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}
```

</details>

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def is_palindrome_clean_then_reverse(s: str) -> bool:
    cleaned = [c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()]
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]


def is_palindrome_the_one_to_remember(s: str) -> bool:
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True

APPROACHES = [
    is_palindrome_clean_then_reverse,
    is_palindrome_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# skipping non-alphanumerics without comparing them — ' ' is all skip, '0P' is the case-folding trap
CASES = [
    lambda: ("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama",),
    lambda: ("race a car",),
    lambda: (" ",),
    lambda: ("ab, BA",),
    lambda: ("0P",),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<35} -> {answers}")
```
